meta.title: Who really said "Well, I don't know as I want a lawyer to tell me what I cannot do. I hire him to tell how to do what I want to do"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: J. P. Morgan's lawyer line is real but second-hand: Ida Tarbell printed it in 1925 as Judge Elbert Gary's recollection, and the popular version drops a word.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Well, I don't know as I want a lawyer to tell me what I cannot do. I hire him to tell how to do what I want to do'?
meta.ogDescription: Documented, but at one remove: Tarbell's 1925 Gary biography is the source, and it reads 'tell me how,' not 'tell how.'

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Documented, but at one remove. Ida Tarbell prints the line in her 1925 biography of Judge Elbert H. Gary as Gary’s own recollection of a rebuke Morgan gave him — and Tarbell’s text reads “I hire him to tell me how to do what I want to do,” one word longer than the version everyone quotes.

source.heading: Where the line is actually printed

docMeta.dd: The Life of Elbert H. Gary: The Story of Steel
D. Appleton and Company, New York and London, 1925 — page 81
Second-hand — Judge Gary’s recollection, printed after Morgan’s death in 1913

source.excerpt:
Judge Gary was not unknown to the famous banker. Some months before this, when in New York on business, he had been called in by one of Mr. Morgan’s counsel to give his opinion on a railroad matter involving Illinois law and practice. “I don’t think you can do that legally, Mr. Morgan,” Judge Gary had said when the case had been stated.

“Well,” said Mr. Morgan — and his “well” was always a challenging, often a terrifying expletive — “I don’t know as I want a lawyer to tell me what I cannot do. I hire him to tell me how to do what I want to do.”

“Tell me your purpose,” the Judge replied, “and I will see what can be done.”
trail: Started at Wikiquote ↗, which files the line under Attributed and points to Ida Tarbell’s Life of Elbert H. Gary — but gives no page, and reproduces the shortened “tell how” wording. Quote Investigator has not examined this one.
Pulled the full 1925 D. Appleton first edition from the Internet Archive ↗ and found the exchange on page 81, in the chapter “Gary Goes into Iron and Steel” — reading “I hire him to tell me how.”
Compared the aggregators: Goodreads ↗ prints the shortened form with no source at all, while LibQuotes ↗ keeps the “me” and does name Tarbell’s 1925 book.
Checked the two men against Wikipedia’s articles on J. P. Morgan ↗ and Elbert Henry Gary ↗: Morgan died in 1913, and Gary chaired the board of the U.S. Steel Corporation formed in 1901.

author.name: J. P. Morgan
author.heading: J. P. Morgan
author.metaLine: 1837–1913 · American financier, banker and art collector
author.bio: J. P. Morgan was the most powerful private financier the United States has produced — founder of J.P. Morgan & Company, and the man who in 1901 assembled U.S. Steel, described as the world’s first billion-dollar company. During the Panic of 1907 he personally marshalled New York’s bank and trust executives to halt the collapse, because there was no central bank to do it. He was also a formidable art collector — and, on this evidence, not a man who enjoyed hearing what the law would not let him do.

cite.sourceCitation: Ida M. Tarbell, The Life of Elbert H. Gary: The Story of Steel (New York: D. Appleton and Company, 1925), 81. This is the source to which the attribution traces; Tarbell reports the remark as Judge Gary’s recollection of a conversation, not from a contemporary record, and her text reads “I hire him to tell me how to do what I want to do.”

misattribution.heading: What went wrong in transit
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is credited with this one — the trouble is what happened to it on the way to the quote sites. The line left a 1925 biography as one half of a two-man exchange and arrived online as a free-floating Morgan maxim, a word short.

items.who: “I hire him to tell how to do what I want to do”
items.why: This is the form Goodreads ↗ carries, and the form Wikiquote ↗ reproduces too. Tarbell’s printed text reads “I hire him to tell me how to do what I want to do.” The missing pronoun looks like a copying artefact rather than a second thing Morgan said.

In Tarbell’s account ↗ it is a retort, not a motto. Judge Gary had just told him “I don’t think you can do that legally, Mr. Morgan,” and Gary’s reply — “Tell me your purpose, and I will see what can be done” — is the half that always gets left off.

Morgan died in 1913; the remark reaches us only through a 1925 biography whose subject, Judge Gary, was the other man in the room and sat for interviews with the author. That is why Wikiquote ↗ lists it under “Attributed” rather than among its sourced quotations — and why we do the same.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is solid enough to print, and it is one word off. Ida Tarbell’s The Life of Elbert H. Gary ↗ (1925), page 81, is where it lives — as Judge Gary’s memory of what Morgan said to him some months before the 1897 wire-and-nail negotiations.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: Elbert H. Gary was a county judge from Wheaton, Illinois who had just told the most powerful banker in America that his plan would not stand up. Morgan’s answer — delivered with a “well” that Tarbell describes as always challenging and often terrifying — is close to a founding statement of transactional lawyering: counsel is not there to say no, it is there to find the route to yes.

What actually makes the anecdote work is Gary’s comeback, which the quote sites never carry. He did not argue the point; he asked what Morgan was trying to achieve, then told him there was a legal way to get there. Tarbell writes that the banker was immensely pleased and never forgot it — and in 1901 it was Gary who chaired the board of the U.S. Steel Corporation that Morgan assembled.
context.detailsSummary: A note on who wrote this down
detailsBody: Ida M. Tarbell was the muckraker whose History of the Standard Oil Company helped break up Rockefeller’s trust, which makes her an unexpected biographer for a steel executive. She explains the arrangement in her own preface: D. Appleton invited her to write the book, Gary agreed to hand over his biographical papers and open the Corporation’s records, and he sat with her at length to “discuss with me the events of his life.”

That is the reason to read this particular anecdote carefully rather than dismiss it. It is well sourced in the sense that it comes from a named participant in a book he cooperated with — and it is weak in the sense that the participant is the man the story flatters, recalling a remark made roughly three decades earlier by someone who had been dead since 1913.

sourcesVerified.claim: Ida M. Tarbell's The Life of Elbert H. Gary: The Story of Steel (D. Appleton and Company, 1925) prints on page 81, in the chapter "Gary Goes into Iron and Steel", Morgan saying: "I don't know as I want a lawyer to tell me what I cannot do. I hire him to tell me how to do what I want to do." — preceded by Gary's "I don't think you can do that legally, Mr. Morgan" and followed by "Tell me your purpose, and I will see what can be done." Tarbell also describes Morgan's "well" as "always a challenging, often a terrifying expletive", places the exchange some months before the 1897 wire-and-nail combination talks, and states in her preface that Gary opened his papers and the Corporation's records to her and sat for interviews.

English Wikiquote lists the line in its "Attributed" section for J. P. Morgan with the note "Attributed by Ida Tarbell in Life of Elbert H. Gary", and reproduces it as "I hire him to tell how to do what I want to do" — without the word "me".
Goodreads displays the quote as "Well, I don't know as I want a lawyer to tell me what I cannot do. I hire him to tell how to do what I want to do." with no book or source citation.

LibQuotes gives the wording with "I hire him to tell me how to do what I want to do" and cites it to The Life of Elbert H. Gary by Ida M. Tarbell (1925), and gives Morgan's dates as born 17 April 1837, died 31 March 1913.
AZQuotes displays the quote in the shortened "I hire him to tell how to do what I want to do" form and cites Ida M. Tarbell, The Life of Elbert H. Gary (1925).

J. P. Morgan lived 17 April 1837 to 31 March 1913, founded J.P. Morgan & Company, orchestrated the 1901 formation of U.S. Steel described as the world's first billion-dollar company, organised the banker rescue during the Panic of 1907, and was an art collector.

Elbert Henry Gary (born 8 October 1846, died 15 August 1927) was a lawyer and DuPage County judge (1882-1890) who was a founder of U.S. Steel in 1901 alongside J. P. Morgan and served as chairman of its board of directors and finance committee.

The Internet Archive holds Ida M. Tarbell's The Life of Elbert H. Gary: The Story of Steel, D. Appleton, 1925, as an openly readable scan (no access restriction), matching the printed title page reading "D. APPLETON AND COMPANY, NEW YORK :: LONDON :: MCMXXV" and copyright notice "Copyright, 1925, by the S. S. McClure Company".
